summary: For ages 12–14: compare the 'Big Five' mass extinctions (End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, K-Pg), attach each to its main proposed kill mechanism (noting that some mechanisms, such as volcanism and ocean anoxia, appear in more than one event), rank the End-Permian as most severe, and — crucially — understand each extinction as reset-and-rediversify: catastrophe clears ecological space that later enables adaptive radiations (e.g. mammals after the K-Pg, a lineage that eventually included humans). Learners place events on a geologic timeline, trace cause→collapse→recovery, and correct the assumption that the famous K-Pg was the biggest.
misconceptions: 'The K-Pg (dinosaur) extinction was the biggest' — the End-Permian was far more severe.
'All mass extinctions had the same cause (asteroids)' — mechanisms differ (glaciation, anoxia, volcanism, impact).
'Extinction is purely destructive' — it also opens niches enabling adaptive radiations.
'Mass extinctions happen instantly' — some unfolded over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years.
'Species that survived were the strongest/most advanced' — survival often reflected small size, generalism or luck, not superiority.

activities.title: Run the crash and the recovery on a biodiversity timeline
steps: Work with a biodiversity-through-time curve stretched across the geologic timeline, with the five Big Five events marked as dips.

Select an event and link it to its own kill mechanism: End-Ordovician (glaciation and sea-level fall), Late Devonian (ocean anoxia), End-Permian (Siberian Traps mega-volcanism → warming, acidification, anoxia, ~252 Mya), End-Triassic (volcanism/CAMP), K-Pg (asteroid impact).
If a dynamic model is available, trigger each mechanism and watch the diversity curve drop — deepest at the End-Permian (~90% of species) — so severity is seen, not just asserted.

For each event, move to a 'recovery' phase and watch or trace surviving groups radiate into emptied niches; after the K-Pg, follow small mammals fanning out into the niches non-avian dinosaurs left, a radiation that over tens of millions of years produced a lineage eventually including humans — a plausible consequence of the clearing, not a guaranteed one.
Use a compare-mode to overlay two events' severity and mechanism side by side and state which was more severe and why.
Write one sentence capturing the two-sided idea: a mass extinction is both an ending and a reset that enables re-diversification.
activities.insight: Mass extinctions differ in cause and severity; each catastrophe both removes a large fraction of species and opens ecological space, so extinction and the later adaptive radiation, which typically took millions of years to unfold, are linked parts of the same reset-and-rediversify story.

activities.title: Annotated diversity curve: read each dip
steps: Examine a single annotated diversity-through-time graph with the five dips marked.
For each dip, identify its date, approximate severity (% species lost), kill mechanism, and the radiation that followed.
Mark which dip is deepest and explain why the End-Permian is deepest despite the K-Pg being better known.
Explain in your own words what 'radiated afterward' means for at least one event.
activities.insight: A clear comparison of dates, severities, mechanisms and recoveries can be read directly from a well-labelled curve, reinforcing that the five events differ and each is followed by diversification.

activities.title: Sequence, match and explain (check understanding)
steps: Order the Big Five chronologically with approximate dates.
Match each event to its main kill mechanism.
State which extinction was most severe (End-Permian) and justify the ranking.
Explain the extinction→radiation logic using the K-Pg→mammals→(eventually) humans chain in a written or spoken response, not just a selected option.
activities.insight: Being able to sequence, match, rank severity and explain the extinction→radiation link demonstrates the full concept rather than isolated recall.

activities.title: Ask a palaeobiologist (perspective extension)
steps: Pose questions a palaeobiologist could discuss, e.g. 'Why did roughly 90% of species die in the Great Dying?' or 'Are we entering a sixth mass extinction?'
After discussing, relate the answer back to the comparative timeline: how does this event's cause and severity sit against the others?
Consider why survivors were often small, generalist or simply lucky rather than 'the strongest or most advanced'.
activities.insight: Expert discussion can add depth and real-world relevance (severity drivers, the possibility of a current sixth extinction, the role of luck in survival) that complements the core comparative-causal analysis.

checkQuestion: The K-Pg asteroid extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs is the most famous mass extinction. Was it the most severe one Earth has ever had? And is a mass extinction purely a disaster, or can it also do something for life afterwards? Explain.
checkAnswer: No — the End-Permian extinction (~252 million years ago), linked to the Siberian Traps volcanic eruptions, was far more severe, wiping out around 90% of species. And while catastrophic, mass extinctions also clear ecological space: after the K-Pg removed the non-avian dinosaurs, mammals radiated and diversified, eventually including us. Destruction and later diversification are two sides of the same event.
